title: The crow and the swan
hookLine: Shalya keeps his promise with a story about a crow and a swan
carry: ahamkara boasts; the hamsa flies straight

cards: As the chariot rolls out, Karna is in high spirits. Whoever shows me where Arjuna is, he calls across the field, I'll reward him richly. Beside him, holding the reins, Shalya laughs.
Save your gifts, he says, in effect. You'll see Arjuna soon enough, and you won't enjoy it. Karna boasts again.
Shalya mocks again: two proud men in one small chariot, the army watching. Then Shalya stops arguing and does something sharper. He tells a story.

teach.h: I KNOW ONE WAY TO FLY
teach.b: In Ganguli's English, it goes like this. A crow lived in a merchant's house, and the merchant's children fed it the leftovers from their plates.
One day some swans came by, and the crow challenged them: I know more ways to fly than you can name. A swan answered simply: I know one way. They set out over the ocean.
The crow showed off, diving and wheeling, every trick it knew. The swan flew straight. Far out over the water the crow grew tired, sank toward the waves with nowhere to land, and begged for help.
The swan lifted it onto its back and carried it back to land. Then Shalya turns to Karna.
You, he says, are that crow, fed on the leftovers of Dhritarashtra's sons, and Arjuna is the swan. The promise to Yudhishthira, kept. Karna answers with hard words and rides on.
Shalya meant it cruelly, but Hindus hear more, because the swan, the hamsa, is no ordinary bird to them. The hamsa carries Saraswati, the goddess of wisdom, in countless pictures.

An old saying holds that a hamsa can separate milk from water, so it stands for viveka, discernment, telling the real from the false. The greatest saints are even called paramahamsa, the supreme swan.
Read in that light, many teachers say, the crow is the other side: ahamkara, the ego, literally the I-maker, puffed up and showing every trick. Ahamkara gets tired far out over the water.
The hamsa needs one way, flown straight, and when the boaster sinks, it lifts him up.
So the next time you feel the need to prove every trick you know, the old picture asks: crow, or swan?

how: Shalya's fable of the crow and the swan is retold in readings of the Karna Parva and in collections of Mahabharata stories, where it can travel on its own as a story about pride.

o: the driver who tells a fable to wear a warrior down
the archer whom Shalya's fable casts as the swan

the swan lifts the exhausted crow onto its back and carries it back to land.
Shalya told the story to cheer Karna on

games.q: you're the swan, far out over the ocean. the crow who mocked you is sinking toward the waves, begging for help. what do you do?
o: lift it onto your back and carry it home.
circle and remind it of its boasting.
games.why: the swan carries the crow back to land: the hamsa's clear mind has no need to gloat. the sting is for Karna, not the crow: Shalya says Karna is that crow.

practice: Let your breath find one simple path: in through the nose, out slowly. Some Hindu yoga traditions hear the breath itself as a mantra: so on the way in, ham on the way out. So'ham, I am That.
Turned around, it becomes hamsa, the swan. Try it silently for a few breaths, and when your mind starts showing off, come back to that one straight line.
If you pray, let the breath be your prayer; if not, the plain breath is enough.

wordCard.voice: Karna. The commander who rides out boasting, and hears his driver tell him he's the crow, and rides on anyway.

orig.note: swan: Saraswati's bird and a sign of discernment, and the swan in Shalya's story that flies one way.

carryVoice: Your line: ahamkara boasts; the hamsa flies straight. The swan never needed the tricks. See you tomorrow.
